On the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem

Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu Address: Shanghai Center for Mathematical Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai, China, 200433 Email address: linweinan@fudan.edu.cn Address: Shanghai Center for Mathematical Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai, China, 200433 Email address: wangguozhen@fudan.edu.cn Address: UCLA Department of Mathematics, Los Angeles, CA 90095-1555, USA Email address: xuzhouli@ucla.edu Dedicated to Mark Mahowald
Abstract.

We prove that the element h62h_{6}^{2} is a permanent cycle in the Adams spectral sequence. As a result, we establish the existence of smooth framed manifolds with Kervaire invariant one in dimension 126, thereby resolving the final case of the Kervaire invariant problem.

Combining this result with the theorems of Browder, Mahowald–Tangora, Barratt–Jones–Mahowald, and Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel, we conclude that smooth framed manifolds with Kervaire invariant one exist in and only in dimensions 2,6,14,30,622,6,14,30,62, and 126126.

1. Introduction

For a smooth framed manifold in dimension 4​k+24k+2, the Kervaire invariant, taking values in 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, determines whether the manifold could be converted into a homotopy sphere via surgery – it takes value 0 if the manifold can be converted to a homotopy sphere and 1 otherwise. Formally speaking, the Kervaire invariant is defined as the Arf invariant of the quadratic refinement of the intersection pairing in the cohomology of the manifold with 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} coefficients. Using this invariant, Kervaire [33] discovered a PL-manifold in dimension 10 that does not admit any smooth structure.

The Kervaire invariant problem seeks to identify the dimensions in which there exist framed smooth manifolds with Kervaire invariant one. In these dimensions, exactly half of the cobordism classes of framed manifolds have Kervaire invariant one, and the other half have Kervaire invariant 0. The Kervaire invariant problem is closely related to many problems in differential topology, especially Kervaire–Milnor’s classification theorem [34] on exotic smooth structures on spheres.

In this paper we prove the following Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 1.1.

There exist framed manifolds of Kervaire invariant one in dimension 126.

Together with previous results by Browder [10], Mahowald–Tangora [44], Barratt–Jones–Mahowald [4], and Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel [23], this is the last case of the Kervaire invariant problem.

Corollary 1.2.

The dimensions that there exist framed manifolds of Kervaire invariant one are 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, and 126.

In dimensions 2, 6, and 14, the product of spheres S1×S1,S3×S3,S7×S7S^{1}\times S^{1},\ S^{3}\times S^{3},S^{7}\times S^{7} can be framed to have Kervarie invariant one. In dimension 30, an explicit framed manifold of Kervarie invariant one was constructed by J.Jones in [32]. For dimensions 62 and 126, we would like to comment that no explicit manifold of Kervarie invariant one was known, although 50%50\% of all framed manifolds in these two dimensions have Kervarie invariant one.

Our Theorem 1.1 is a consequence of Browder’s theorem (Theorem 1.3) and the following main theorem of this paper, Theorem 1.4.

Theorem 1.3 (Browder [10]).

There exist framed manifolds in dimension nn of Kervaire invariant one if and only if

  1. (1)

    n=2j+1−2n=2^{j+1}-2, and

  2. (2)

    the element hj2h_{j}^{2} in the Adams spectral sequence survives to the E∞E_{\infty}-page.

The Adams spectral sequence [1] converges to the stable homotopy groups of spheres, which, by Pontryagin’s theorem, correspond to framed manifolds up to framed cobordism. When the element hj2h_{j}^{2} survives (see below for an introduction to the Adams spectral sequence and the element hj2h_{j}^{2}), the homotopy classes it detects are denoted by θj∈π2j+1−2\theta_{j}\in\pi_{2^{j+1}-2}. Browder showed that these classes correspond to framed manifolds with Kervaire invariant one.

Theorem 1.4 (Theorem 7.1).

The element h62h_{6}^{2} survives to the E∞E_{\infty}-page in the Adams spectral sequence.

In addition to Theorem 1.1, further implications of Theorem 1.4, particularly in manifold topology and unstable homotopy theory, can be found in [47, 42, 23, 3], among others.

Recall that the 2-primary Adams spectral sequence has the following form.

E2s,t=ExtAs,t​(𝔽2,𝔽2)⟹πt−s​S0,E_{2}^{s,t}=\mathrm{Ext}^{s,t}_{A}(\mathbb{F}_{2},\mathbb{F}_{2})\Longrightarrow\pi_{t-s}{S^{0}},
dr:Ers,t⟶Ers+r,t+r−1.d_{r}:E_{r}^{s,t}\longrightarrow E_{r}^{s+r,t+r-1}.

Here the E2E_{2}-page is the cohomology of the mod 2 Steenrod algebra A, S0S^{0} is the 2-completed sphere spectrum, and the spectral sequence converges to the 2-completed stable homotopy groups of spheres. In general, for a spectrum XX, its H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-Adams spectral sequence is denoted by Er∗,∗​(X)E_{r}^{*,*}(X), converging to the 2-completed homotopy groups of XX.

For the sphere, Adams [1] computed the Adams 11-line:

ExtA1,t​(𝔽2,𝔽2)={𝔽2,if​t=2j​for some​j≥0,0,otherwise.\mathrm{Ext}^{1,t}_{A}(\mathbb{F}_{2},\mathbb{F}_{2})=\begin{cases}\mathbb{F}_{2},\ \text{if}\ t=2^{j}\ \text{for some}\ j\geq 0,\\ 0,\ \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Denote by hjh_{j} the generator of 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} in the bidegree (s,t)=(1,2j)(s,t)=(1,2^{j}). Adams [2] proved that the element hjh_{j} survives in the Adams spectral sequence if and only if j≥3j\geq 3, resolving the famous Hopf invariant problem. In fact, Adams proved that

d2​(hj)=h0​hj−12≠0,for​j≥4.d_{2}(h_{j})=h_{0}h_{j-1}^{2}\neq 0,\ \text{for}\ j\geq 4.

The Kervaire invariant element hj2h_{j}^{2} lives on the Adams 2-line, which is generated by elements of the form {hi​hj}\{h_{i}h_{j}\} that are subject to the relations hi​hi+1=0h_{i}h_{i+1}=0. Notably, h62h_{6}^{2} was the last unknown element on the Adams 2-line whose survival in the Adams spectral sequence remained uncertain prior to our work. As a corollary of Theorem 1.4, we have:

Corollary 1.5.

On the Adams 2-line, the only non-trivial elements that survive in the Adams spectral sequence are:

h0​h2,h0​h3,h2​h4,h1​hj​(j≥3),hj2​(j≤6).h_{0}h_{2},\ h_{0}h_{3},\ h_{2}h_{4},\ h_{1}h_{j}\ (j\geq 3),\ h_{j}^{2}\ (j\leq 6).
Proof.

From Adams’s Hopf invariant one differentials, Lin’s computations of the Adams 4-line [40], and the Leibniz rule, we know that the only elements that survive to the Adams E3E_{3}-page are

h0​h2,h0​h3,h2​h4,h2​h5,h3​h5,h3​h6,h1​hj​(j≥3),hj2​(j≤6).h_{0}h_{2},\ h_{0}h_{3},\ h_{2}h_{4},\ h_{2}h_{5},\ h_{3}h_{5},\ h_{3}h_{6},\ h_{1}h_{j}\ (j\geq 3),\ h_{j}^{2}\ (j\leq 6).

May [45] proved that the first three elements and hj2h_{j}^{2} for j≤3j\leq 3 survive. Mahowald–Tangora [44] proved that h2​h5h_{2}h_{5} supports a nonzero d3d_{3}-differential, h3​h5h_{3}h_{5} supports a nonzero d4d_{4}-differential, and h42h_{4}^{2} survives. Isaksen–Wang–Xu [29] proved that h3​h6h_{3}h_{6} supports a nonzero d3d_{3}-differential. Mahowald [43] proved that h1​hjh_{1}h_{j} for j≥3j\geq 3 survive. Barratt–Jones–Mahowald [4] proved that h52h_{5}^{2} survives (see [56, 29] for alternative proofs). Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel [23] proved that hj2h_{j}^{2} supports nonzero differentials for j≥7j\geq 7 (the targets of these differentials are still unknown). Finally, by Theorem 1.4, h62h_{6}^{2} survives. ∎

Before Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel’s proof on the non-existence of θj\theta_{j} for j≥7j\geq 7, Barratt–Jones–Mahowald [3] had an inductive argument trying to establish the existence of all θj\theta_{j}: They proved that if there exists a θj\theta_{j} satisfying 2⋅θj=0,θj2=02\cdot\theta_{j}=0,\ \theta_{j}^{2}=0, then there exists a θj+1\theta_{j+1} satisfying 2⋅θj+1=02\cdot\theta_{j+1}=0. In particular, the problem of whether a θj+1\theta_{j+1} of order 2 exists is known as the strong Kervaire invariant problem. It was known that 2⋅θj=02\cdot\theta_{j}=0 for j≤5j\leq 5 (see [44] for j=4j=4 and [56, 29] for j=5j=5). Although we prove that θ6\theta_{6} exists in this paper, the following questions are still open:

Question 1.6.

Does there exist a θ6\theta_{6} that has order 2?

Question 1.7.

Does there exist a θ5\theta_{5} such that θ52=0\theta_{5}^{2}=0?

By Barratt–Jones–Mahowald’s theorem [3], if the answer to Question 1.7 is positive, then it would imply our Theorem 1.4 and a positive answer to Question 1.6. We plan to study these questions in a future project.

As suggested by the proof of Corollary 1.5, computation of differentials in the Adams spectral sequence has a long history. See Section 2 of [53] for a brief summary at all primes and computations at the prime 2 up to around 60-stem. For more recent computations up to around 90-stem, see [29, 28, 55, 30].

Many methods were introduced to compute differentials in the Adams spectral sequence. We highlight some of the major methods as follows.

  1. (1)

    Multiplicative structure of the Adams E2E_{2}-page and the Leibniz rule.

    By computing the Adams E2E_{2}-page with its multiplicative structure via the May spectral sequence, and comparing with Toda’s unstable computations, May [45] computed all differentials up to the 28-stem.

  2. (2)

    Higher product structure – interactions between Massey products and Toda brackets through Moss’s theorem [48].

  3. (3)

    The Mahowald trick [44], which translates between differentials and extension problems.

    By using both Moss’s theorem and the Mahowald trick, Barratt–Mahowald–Tangora [44, 5] computed all but one differentials up to the 45-stem; The remaining one was computed by Bruner [11] using power operations.

  4. (4)

    Comparison with the motivic Adams spectral sequence via the Betti realization functor [20].

    By comparison via the Betti realization functor, Isaksen [26] gave rigorous arguments for all but one differentials in both the motivic and classical Adams spectral sequence up to the 59-stem; The remaining one was computed by Xu [31] using the higher Leibniz rule for motivic Massey products.

  5. (5)

    Wang–Xu’s ℝ​P∞\mathbb{R}P^{\infty}-method [53].

    Using Lin’s algebraic Kahn–Priddy theorem [39], Wang–Xu introduced a technique to prove Adams differentials inductively using differentials in subquotients of ℝ​P∞\mathbb{R}P^{\infty}, and completed computations of Adams differentials up to the 61-stem. (See also [54] for application of this method on extension problems.)

    There is a nice geometric application of these differentials in stems 60 and 61. The sphere S61S^{61} has a unique smooth structure and it is the last odd dimensional case: The only ones are S1,S3,S5S^{1},\ S^{3},\ S^{5} and S61S^{61}.

  6. (6)

    Gheorghe–Isaksen–Wang–Xu’s motivic cofiber of tau method [22, 29].

    By identifying the algebraicity of the special fiber of a motivic deformation, Gheorghe–Wang–Xu [22] proved that the motivic Adams spectral sequence of the cofiber of tau is isomorphic to the algebraic Novikov spectral sequence for BP∗, which can be completely computed in a large range by Wang’s program [52]. Then differentials in the classical Adams spectral sequence follow from naturality.

    Using this method, together with some others, Isaksen–Wang–Xu [29] computed Adams differentials up to the 90-stem, with only a few exceptions.

  7. (7)

    H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic/filtered spectra method [50, 13, 18, 17].

    The homotopy ring of the H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic sphere [50, 16] can be viewed as a tool to encode homotopical information of the classical Adams spectral sequence, in analog to the relation between the homotopy ring of the ℂ\mathbb{C}-motivic sphere [26] and the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence.

    By studying the H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic sphere, Burklund–Isaksen–Xu [17] proved a few Adams differentials up to the 90-stem that were left out by Isaksen–Wang–Xu [29].

Our strategy for proving our main Theorem 1.4 that h62h_{6}^{2} survives is three-fold.

  • •

    Lin’s Program.

    By establishing the theory of noncommutative Gröbner bases for Steenrod algebras [36], Lin made computer programs that compute Ext groups in a very effective way. We use Lin’s program to compute the Adams E2E_{2}-pages for a vast collection of finite spectra and the maps between them. For a detailed account of the range of Adams E2E_{2} data computed, see [38].

    Building on the theory of secondary Steenrod algebras [6, 49, 19], we also leverage Lin’s program to compute Adams d2d_{2}-for certain finite spectra. Details on the d2d_{2}-differentials we have computed can also be found in [38].

    Additionally, Lin’s program facilitates the propagation of differentials and extensions by employing the Leibniz rule and the naturality of Adams spectral sequences and extension spectral sequences (Definition 2.1).

  • •

    The Generalized Leibniz Rule and the Generalized Mahowald Trick.

    The use of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic/filtered spectra allows us to discuss elements on the Adams EnE_{n}-page as classes in the homotopy groups of certain synthetic spectra [50, 18]. In particular, naturality on synthetic homotopy groups allows us to discuss jump-of-filtration phenomena on any Adams EnE_{n}-page in a rigorous way.

    Using H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra, we develop the Generalized Leibniz Rule (Theorem 6.1) and the Generalized Mahowald Trick (Theorem 6.12), which can be viewed as generalizations of the classical Mahowald’s trick and geometric boundary theorem studies by Ravenel, Behrens and others [51, 8, 41, 14]. We then use them to further propagate differentials from the known ones.

    With the Generalized Leibniz Rule and the Generalized Mahowald Trick, Lin’s program becomes even more powerful, enabling the derivation of additional differentials. The program rigorously verifies the conditions of the relevant theorems and generates human-readable proofs [37] for all differentials computed by the machine. In the Appendix, readers will find tables of Adams differentials that are used in the proof of the main Theorem 1.4.

  • •

    The inductive approach and adhoc arguments near stem 126.

    By studying Barratt–Jones–Mahowald’s inductive approach [3] in the H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic context, Burklund–Xu (Proposition 7.19 of [18]) proved that h62h_{6}^{2} is a permanent cycle in the classical Adams spectral sequence if and only if λ​η​θ52=0\lambda\eta\theta_{5}^{2}=0 in the homotopy group of the synthetic sphere. Here λ\lambda is our notation for the synthetic deformation parameter, and θ5\theta_{5} is any synthetic homotopy class that is detected by h52h_{5}^{2} on the Adams E2E_{2}-page.

    There are 105 additive generators in stem 125 of the classical Adams E2E_{2}-page – these are the potential targets that could be hit by a nonzero differential from h62h_{6}^{2}. Using Lin’s program and the inductive approach, we can rule out 101 out of the 105 elements.

    By further applying the Generalized Leibniz Rule and the Generalized Mahowald Trick, we can reduce the possibility of a nonzero differential supported by h62h_{6}^{2} to only one case: A nonzero d12d_{12} hits a certain element in stem 125, filtration 14 (see Proposition 7.8(2)). A necessary condition for this nonzero d12d_{12} is an η\eta-extension from stem 124, filtration 10 to stem 125, filtration 14 (see Proposition 7.8(5)).

    By a careful inspection of the homotopy groups of the synthetic sphere (and on certain Adams EnE_{n}-pages) near stem 126, we use adhoc arguments to prove that the η\eta-extension in the previous paragraph cannot happen (see Proposition 7.9) and conclude that h62h_{6}^{2} survives in the Adams spectral sequence.

Organization. In Section 2, we setup and discuss properties of an extension spectral sequence for a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y between two spectra, whose E0E_{0}-page is isomorphic to the direct sum of E∞E_{\infty}-pages of the Adams spectral sequences of XX and YY, and differentials correspond to f∗:π∗​X→π∗​Yf_{*}:\pi_{*}X\to\pi_{*}Y, filtered by the Adams filtration. This setup allows us to discuss the jump-of-filtration phenomena rigorously. In Section 3, we recall and discuss certain properties of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra. In Section 4, we discuss the extension spectral sequence from Section 2 in the context of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra. In Section 5, we discuss extensions on a classical Adams EnE_{n}-page, defined in terms of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra. In Section 6, using the language of Sections 4 and 5, we develop the Generalized Leibniz Rule and the Generalized Mahowald Trick. In Section 7, we use the inductive approach, and ad hoc arguments prove that h62h_{6}^{2} survives in the Adams spectral sequence. Necessary information of the classical Adams spectral sequence for the final ad hoc arguments is included in the Appendix.

2. A Spectral Sequence for Extensions

In this paper, we assume that all symbols X,Y,Z,W,…X,Y,Z,W,\dots for spectra represent 2-completed connective spectra of finite type. In particular, their H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-Adams spectral sequences converge strongly.

Consider a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y between two spectra and we can construct the following chain complex

0→π∗​X→π∗​fπ∗​Y→00\to\pi_{*}X\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}f}\pi_{*}Y\to 0

whose homology is

ker⁡(π∗​f)⊕coker⁡(π∗​f).\Ker(\pi_{*}f)\oplus\Coker(\pi_{*}f).

We encounter ff-extension problems when analyzing the homotopy groups through the E∞E_{\infty}-pages of the H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-based Adams spectral sequences. To address these extensions, we introduce the following spectral sequence.

Definition 2.1.

For a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y, we define an ff-extension spectral sequence (denoted ff-ESS) as the spectral sequence derived from filtering the above chain complex according to the Adams filtration on π∗\pi_{*}. The E0E_{0}-page of this spectral sequence is isomorphic to the direct sum of E∞E_{\infty}-pages of the Adams spectral sequences of XX and YY:

Es,t0f≅E∞s,t​(X)⊕E∞s,t​(Y)⟹ker⁡(π∗​f)⊕coker⁡(π∗​f)\prescript{f\!}{}{E}_{0}^{s,t}\cong E_{\infty}^{s,t}(X)\oplus E_{\infty}^{s,t}(Y)\Longrightarrow\Ker(\pi_{*}f)\oplus\Coker(\pi_{*}f)

where the d0d_{0}-differential is induced by ff on the E∞E_{\infty}-pages.

Differentials in this spectral sequence has the form

dnf:Es,tnf→Es+n,t+nnf.d_{n}^{f}:\prescript{f\!}{}{E}_{n}^{s,t}\to\prescript{f\!}{}{E}_{n}^{s+n,t+n}.

To prevent confusion between differentials dnd_{n} in the Adams spectral sequence of a spectrum XX and those in the ff-extension spectral sequence, we denote the latter with a superscript, writing them as dnfd_{n}^{f}.

In the remainder of the paper, we denote by AF⁡(f)\mathrm{AF}(f) the Adams filtration of a map ff. Recall that AF⁡(f)≥k\mathrm{AF}(f)\geq k if and only if there exist kk composable maps f1,…,fkf_{1},\ldots,f_{k}, each inducing a trivial map in H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-homology, such that ff is homotopic to the composition fk∘⋯∘f1f_{k}\circ\cdots\circ f_{1} (see [51, Theorem 2.2.14] for example).

Notation 2.2.

Let Zns,tf​(X)⊂E∞s,t​(X)\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}^{s,t}_{n}(X)\subset E^{s,t}_{\infty}(X) be the subgroup consisting of elements for which the ff-extension differentials d0f,…,dnfd^{f}_{0},\dots,d^{f}_{n} vanish. Let Bns,tf​(Y)⊂E∞s,t​(Y)\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s,t}_{n}(Y)\subset E^{s,t}_{\infty}(Y) be the subgroup generated by the sum of images of the ff-extension differentials d0f,…,dnfd^{f}_{0},\dots,d^{f}_{n}. We define B−1s,tf​(Y)=0\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s,t}_{-1}(Y)=0 and Z−1s,tf​(X)=E∞s,t​(X)\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}^{s,t}_{-1}(X)=E^{s,t}_{\infty}(X).

By definition we have

Ens,tf≅Zn−1s,tf​(X)⊕(E∞s,t​(Y)/Bn−1s,tf​(Y)).\prescript{f\!}{}{E}^{s,t}_{n}\cong\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}^{s,t}_{n-1}(X)\oplus\big(E^{s,t}_{\infty}(Y)/\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s,t}_{n-1}(Y)\big).

A nonzero dnfd^{f}_{n} differential takes the form

dnf:Zn−1s,tf​(X)→E∞s+n,t+n​(Y)/Bn−1s+n,t+nf​(Y).d^{f}_{n}:\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}^{s,t}_{n-1}(X)\to E^{s+n,t+n}_{\infty}(Y)/\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s+n,t+n}_{n-1}(Y).

When we write

dnf​(x)=yd^{f}_{n}(x)=y

for x∈E∞s,t​(X)x\in E_{\infty}^{s,t}(X) and y∈E∞s+n,t+n​(Y)y\in E_{\infty}^{s+n,t+n}(Y), it is understood that xx belongs to Zn−1s,tf​(X)\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}^{s,t}_{n-1}(X), and

dnf​(x)=y+Bn−1s+n,t+nf​(Y).d^{f}_{n}(x)=y+\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s+n,t+n}_{n-1}(Y).

Furthermore, we may sometimes write

dnf​(x)≡ymodMd^{f}_{n}(x)\equiv y\mod M

for some subgroup M⊂E∞s+n,t+n​(Y)M\subset E_{\infty}^{s+n,t+n}(Y). This means that

dnf​(x)=y+m+Bn−1s+n,t+nf​(Y)d^{f}_{n}(x)=y+m+\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s+n,t+n}_{n-1}(Y)

for some m∈Mm\in M.

Definition 2.3.

We say there is an ff-extension from x∈E∞s,t​(X)x\in E_{\infty}^{s,t}(X) to y∈E∞s+n,t+n​(Y)y\in E_{\infty}^{s+n,t+n}(Y) if dnf​(x)=yd_{n}^{f}(x)=y in the ff-ESS. We say this ff-extension is essential if yy is nontrivial in the EnE_{n}-page of the ff-ESS, or equivalently

y∉Bn−1s+n,t+nf​(Y).y\notin\prescript{f\!}{}{B}^{s+n,t+n}_{n-1}(Y).

Otherwise we refer to it as inessential.

Notation 2.4.

For x∈E∞s,t​(X)x\in E_{\infty}^{s,t}(X), we denote by {x}\{x\} the set of all classes in πt−s​X\pi_{t-s}X that are detected by xx. We use [x][x] to refer to a specific class or a general class in {x}\{x\}, with the choice understood from the context.

Proposition 2.5.

Consider f:X→Yf:X\to Y, x∈E∞s,t​(X)x\in E_{\infty}^{s,t}(X), y∈E∞s+n,t+n​(Y)y\in E_{\infty}^{s+n,t+n}(Y) and y′∈E∞s+m,t+m​(Y)y^{\prime}\in E_{\infty}^{s+m,t+m}(Y) for m,n≥0m,n\geq 0.

  1. (1)

    There is an ff-extension from xx to yy, i.e., dnf​(x)=yd_{n}^{f}(x)=y in the ff-ESS if and only if there is a class [x]∈{x}[x]\in\{x\} such that f⁡[x]∈{y}f[x]\in\{y\}.

    An ff-extension from xx to yy is inessential, i.e., yy is trivial in the EnE_{n}-page of the ff-ESS if and only if there exists an element x′∈E∞s+a,t+a​(X)x^{\prime}\in E_{\infty}^{s+a,t+a}(X) for 0<a≤n0<a\leq n such that we have an essential differential dn−af​(x′)=yd_{n-a}^{f}(x^{\prime})=y. Equivalently, there exists a class [x′]∈{x′}⊂π∗​X[x^{\prime}]\in\{x^{\prime}\}\subset\pi_{*}X with AF(x′)>(x^{\prime})>AF(x)(x), such that f⁡[x′]∈{y}f[x^{\prime}]\in\{y\}.

  3. (3)

    Suppose we have an ff-extension from xx to both yy and y′y^{\prime}.

    1. (a)

Proposition 2.10.

An ff-extension from xx to yy has no crossing in the range AF≥p\mathrm{AF}\geq p if and only if for all [x]∈{x}[x]\in\{x\} such that AF⁡(f⁡[x])≥p\mathrm{AF}(f[x])\geq p we have f⁡[x]∈{y}f[x]\in\{y\}. In particular, we have

  1. (1)

    An ff-extension from xx to yy has no crossing if and only if for all [x]∈{x}[x]\in\{x\} we have f⁡[x]∈{y}f[x]\in\{y\}.

  2. (2)

    An ff-extension dnf​(x)=0d_{n}^{f}(x)=0 has no crossing if and only if for all [x]∈{x}[x]\in\{x\},

    AF⁡(f⁡[x])>AF⁡(x)+n.\mathrm{AF}(f[x])>\mathrm{AF}(x)+n.
  3. (3)

    If AF⁡(f)=n\mathrm{AF}(f)=n, then all dnfd^{f}_{n}-differentials have no crossing in the ff-ESS.

Proof.

First we prove the only if part. Assume by contradiction that there exists [x]∈{x}[x]\in\{x\} such that f⁡[x]=[y′]∉{y}f[x]=[y^{\prime}]\notin\{y\} is detected by y′∈E∞​(Y)y^{\prime}\in E_{\infty}(Y) with AF⁡(y′)≥p\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})\geq p. Then there is an ff extension from xx to y′y^{\prime}. By Proposition 2.5 (3), y′y^{\prime} (if AF⁡(y)>AF⁡(y′)\mathrm{AF}(y)>\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})) or y−y′y-y^{\prime} (if AF⁡(y)=AF⁡(y′)\mathrm{AF}(y)=\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})) or yy (if AF⁡(y)<AF⁡(y′)\mathrm{AF}(y)<\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})) should be hit by a shorter dfd^{f} differential. This shorter differential is a crossing of the ff-extension from xx to yy that hits AF≥p\mathrm{AF}\geq p, which is a contradiction. Now we prove the if part. Assume that the ff-extension has a crossing from x′x^{\prime} to y′y^{\prime} with p≤AF⁡(y′)≤AF⁡(y)p\leq\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})\leq\mathrm{AF}(y). Then there exists [x′]∈{x′}[x^{\prime}]\in\{x^{\prime}\} such that f⁡([x′])∈{y′}f([x^{\prime}])\in\{y^{\prime}\}. Note that [x]+[x′]∈{x}[x]+[x^{\prime}]\in\{x\} since AF⁡(x′)>AF⁡(x)\mathrm{AF}(x^{\prime})>\mathrm{AF}(x), we have

f⁡([x]+[x′])=f⁡([x])+f⁡([x′])=[y]+[y′]∈{{y′} if ​AF​(y′)<AF⁡(y){y+y′} if ​AF​(y′)=AF⁡(y).f([x]+[x^{\prime}])=f([x])+f([x^{\prime}])=[y]+[y^{\prime}]\in\begin{cases}\{y^{\prime}\}&\text{ if }\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})<\mathrm{AF}(y)\\ \{y+y^{\prime}\}&\text{ if }\mathrm{AF}(y^{\prime})=\mathrm{AF}(y).\\ \end{cases}

However, by assumption we should have f⁡([x]+[x′])∈{y}f([x]+[x^{\prime}])\in\{y\} and it is contradictory to the equation above in either case.

Hence the main statement is true. Part (1) (2) are special cases of the main statement and Part (3) holds for degree reasons. ∎

and Corollary 2.15.

Proposition 2.20.

Suppose that the sequence of spectra

X→𝑓Y→𝑔ZX\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z

induces a sequence of homotopy groups

π∗​X→π∗​fπ∗​Y→π∗​gπ∗​Z\pi_{*}X\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}f}\pi_{*}Y\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}g}\pi_{*}Z

that is exact in π∗​Y\pi_{*}Y. Then all permanent cycles in E∞∗,∗​(Y)E^{*,*}_{\infty}(Y) of the gg-ESS are boundaries in the ff-ESS.

Proof.

If we consider the following sequence

(2.21) 0→π∗​X→π∗​fπ∗​Y→π∗​gπ∗​Z→00\to\pi_{*}X\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}f}\pi_{*}Y\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}g}\pi_{*}Z\to 0

and treat it as a chain complex filtered by the Adams filtration, we obtain an extension spectral sequence comprising dfd^{f} and dgd^{g} differentials. The abutment of this spectral sequence, when projected onto the YY component, is zero. Therefor, all permanent dgd^{g}-cycles are killed by dfd^{f}-differentials.

Again we offer another proof via homotopy groups. Assume that y∈E∞∗,∗​(Y)y\in E^{*,*}_{\infty}(Y) is a permanent dgd^{g} cycle. By the convergence of ESS we know that it detects an gg-torsion [y]∈{y}[y]\in\{y\} with g⁡([y])=0g([y])=0. Hence there exists [x]∈π∗​X[x]\in\pi_{*}X such that f⁡([x])=[y]f([x])=[y] by exactness. Assume that [x][x] is detected by x∈E∞∗,∗​(X)x\in E^{*,*}_{\infty}(X). Then there exists an ff extension from xx to yy. ∎

Corollary 2.19 and Proposition 2.20 are particularly useful because they provide numerous potential applications whenever we have a cofiber sequence of the form

X→𝑓Y→𝑔C​f→ℎΣ​XX\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Cf\xrightarrow{h}\Sigma X

These results can also be implemented in a computer program to facilitate their application.

3. H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra

In Section 2, we explored classical extension problems in the context of commutative diagrams and cofiber sequences of spectra, framed in terms of the extension spectral sequence. The power of the extension spectral sequence can be further enhanced by generalizing and applying it to the category of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra, a topic we will discuss in Section 4.

In this section, we recall some recent work of Pstragowski [50] and Appendix A of Burklund–Hahn–Senger [16] on EE-synthetic spectra, which is strongly motivated by the work of Hu–Kriz–Ormsby [25], Isaksen [26], Gheorghe–Wang–Xu [22], and Gheorghe–Isaksen–Krause–Ricka [21] on the ℂ\mathbb{C}-motivic spectra. We will specialize some of these results to H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra, refining and highlighting specific properties.

The stable, presentable, symmetric monoidal ∞\infty-category SynH​𝔽2\mathrm{Syn}_{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}} of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra is constructed in [50], along with a functor

ν:Sp→SynH​𝔽2,\nu:\mathrm{Sp}\to\mathrm{Syn}_{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}},

from the ∞\infty-category of spectra Sp\mathrm{Sp}. This functor is lax symmetric monoidal and preserves filtered colimits. However, ν\nu does not generally preserve cofiber sequences. Instead, the following holds.

Proposition 3.1 ([50, Lemma 4.23]).

Suppose that

X→𝑓Y→𝑔ZX\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z

is a cofiber sequence of spectra. Then

ν​X→ν​fν​Y→ν​gν​Z\nu X\xrightarrow{\nu f}\nu Y\xrightarrow{\nu g}\nu Z

is a cofiber sequence of H​𝔽2{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}-synthetic spectra if and only if

0→H​𝔽2∗​X→H​𝔽2∗​fH​𝔽2∗​Y→H​𝔽2∗​gH​𝔽2∗​Z→00\to{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}_{*}X\xrightarrow{{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}_{*}f}{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}_{*}Y\xrightarrow{{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}_{*}g}{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}_{*}Z\to 0

is a short exact sequence.

Definition 3.2 ([50, Definition 4.6]).

The bigraded spheres Ss,wS^{s,w} are the synthetic spectra defined by Σs−w​ν​(Sw)\Sigma^{s-w}\nu(S^{w}).

Definition 3.3 ([50, Definition 4.27]).

The natural comparison map

S0,−1=Σ​ν​(S−1)→ν⁡(Σ​S−1)=S0,0S^{0,-1}=\Sigma\nu(S^{-1})\to\nu(\Sigma S^{-1})=S^{0,0}

in the category of H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra is denoted by λ∈π0,−1​S0,0\lambda\in\pi_{0,-1}S^{0,0}. We denote by S0,0/λS^{0,0}/\lambda the cofiber of λ\lambda. In general for synthetic XX the following

λ∧i​dX:Σ0,−1​X→X.\lambda\wedge id_{X}:\Sigma^{0,-1}X\to X.

is a natural transformation and by abuse of notation this map is also denoted by λ\lambda. We denote by X/λX/\lambda the cofiber of λ\lambda which is equivalent to (S0,0/λ)∧X(S^{0,0}/\lambda)\wedge X.

Remark 3.4.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, S0,0/λnS^{0,0}/\lambda^{n} is an E∞E_{\infty}-object in SynH​𝔽2\mathrm{Syn}_{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}} (see [15, Appendix B, C] for example).

Remark 3.5.

The element λ\lambda can be viewed as a parameter of a categorical deformation on SynH​𝔽2\mathrm{Syn}_{\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}} (see [50]).

Inverting λ\lambda, the generic fiber is equivalent to the classical category of 2-completed spectra Sp2∧\textup{Sp}^{\wedge}_{2}. Modding out by λ\lambda, the special fiber is equivalent to Hovey’s derived category [24] of comodules over the mod 2 dual Steenrod algebra 𝒟⁡(A∗​-Comod)\mathcal{D}(A_{*}\textup{-Comod}). Historically, this synthetic deformation is motivated by, and analogous to, the motivic deformation conjectured by Isaksen and proven by Gheorghe–Wang–Xu [22]: Specifically, there exists a map

τ:S0,−1^→S0,0^\tau:\widehat{S^{0,-1}}\rightarrow\widehat{S^{0,0}}

between p-completed motivic spheres. This element τ\tau can be viewed as a parameter of a categorical deformation on the category of cellular objects over S0,0^\widehat{S^{0,0}}.

Inverting τ\tau, the generic fiber is equivalent to the classical category of p-completed spectra Spp∧\textup{Sp}^{\wedge}_{p}. Modding out by τ\tau, the special fiber is equivalent to Hovey’s derived category of comodules over the Hopf algebroid B​P∗​B​PBP_{*}BP.

Theorem 3.6 ([16, Theorem A.8]).

The synthetic Adams spectral sequence for ν​X\nu X

Es,t,w2syn​(ν​X)⟹πt−s,w​(ν​X)\prescript{\mathrm{syn}\!}{}{E}_{2}^{s,t,w}(\nu X)\Longrightarrow\pi_{t-s,w}(\nu X)

has an E2E_{2}-page

E∗,∗,∗2syn​(ν​X)≅E2∗,∗​(X)⊗𝔽2​[λ]\prescript{\mathrm{syn}\!}{}{E}_{2}^{*,*,*}(\nu X)\cong E_{2}^{*,*}(X)\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}[\lambda]

with differentials

dr:Es,t,wrsyn→Es+r,t+r−1,wrsyn.d_{r}:\prescript{\mathrm{syn}\!}{}{E}_{r}^{s,t,w}\to\prescript{\mathrm{syn}\!}{}{E}_{r}^{s+r,t+r-1,w}.

Here E2∗,∗​(X)≅ExtA∗,∗​(X)E_{2}^{*,*}(X)\cong\mathrm{Ext}_{A}^{*,*}(X) is the classical Adams E2E_{2}-page of XX. An element in E2s,t​(X)E_{2}^{s,t}(X) is viewed as having tridegree (s,t,t)(s,t,t) in Es,t,t2syn​(ν​X)\prescript{\mathrm{syn}\!}{}{E}_{2}^{s,t,t}(\nu X), and λ\lambda is in tridegree (0,0,−1)(0,0,-1). Given a classical Adams differential drcl​(x)=yd_{r}^{\mathrm{cl}}(x)=y, the corresponding synthetic differential is dr​(x)=λr−1​yd_{r}(x)=\lambda^{r-1}y, which is λ\lambda-linear, and all synthetic Adams differentials arise in this way.

Remark 3.7.

Here, we use a third grading of the synthetic Adams E2E_{2}-page that differs from [16] but more compatible with [17]. Specifically, we view elements in E2s,t​(X)E_{2}^{s,t}(X) as having tridegree (s,t,t)(s,t,t), instead of (s,t,s)(s,t,s) as in [16]. This choice ensures that differentials and maps preserve the third degree, which proves convenient for the extension spectral sequence in the H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic category in Section 4.

Theorem 3.8 ([16, Theorem A.1]).

The synthetic Adams spectral sequence for ν​X\nu X is isomorphic to the λ\lambda-Bockstein spectral sequence (with no sign difference because we are working over 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2} here). More specifically, we have

  1. (1)

    E2s,t​(X)≅πt−s,t​(ν​X/λ)E_{2}^{s,t}(X)\cong\pi_{t-s,t}(\nu X/\lambda).

  2. (2)

    If we have a classical Adams differential dr​x=yd_{r}x=y for

    x∈E2s,t​(X)≅πt−s,t​(ν​X/λ),x\in E_{2}^{s,t}(X)\cong\pi_{t-s,t}(\nu X/\lambda),

    then xx admits a lift to πt−s,t​(ν​X/λr−1)\pi_{t-s,t}(\nu X/\lambda^{r-1}) whose image under the τ\tau-Bockstein

    ν​X/λr−1→Σ1,−r+1​ν​X/λ\nu X/\lambda^{r-1}\to\Sigma^{1,-r+1}\nu X/\lambda

    is equal to dr​(x)d_{r}(x).

Remark 3.9.

The isomorphism with the λ\lambda-Bockstein spectral sequence in Theorem 3.8 and the correspondence of differentials between the classical and synthetic Adams spectral sequences in Theorem 3.6 can be interpreted as manifestations of the rigidity of the synthetic Adams spectral sequence. This type of rigidity was first observed by Hu–Kriz–Ormsby [25] and Isaksen [26] in the context of the motivic Adams–Novikov spectral sequence, and it was utilized extensively in the work of Gheorghe–Wang–Xu [22]. Subsequently, Burklund–Xu [18] uncovered the rigidity of the motivic Cartan–Eilenberg spectral sequence and performed computations based on this property. See also [27], [13] for applications of this type of rigidity.

Together with Remark 3.5, H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra can be seen as a categorification of the classical Adams spectral sequence, just as cellular motivic spectra can be viewed a categorification of the classical Adams–Novikov spectral sequence.

Remark 3.21.

When AF⁡(f)>1\mathrm{AF}(f)>1, it is often more advantageous to work with C​f~C\tilde{f} rather than C​f^C\hat{f}, as the λ\lambda-Bockstein spectral sequence for C​f~C\tilde{f} corresponds to a modified Adams spectral sequence, which differs from the classical one but may provide additional information. On the other hand, given the equivalence C​f^≃ν​C​fC\hat{f}\simeq\nu Cf from Notation 3.19, the rigidity Theorems 3.6 and 3.8 imply that the synthetic Adams spectral sequence for C​f^C\hat{f} is isomorphic to the λ\lambda-Bockstein spectral sequence, and aligns with the classical Adams spectral sequence for C​fCf. Since the computational data used in this work is based on the classical Adams spectral sequence, we defer the exploration of C​f~C\tilde{f} to future work.

4. Synthetic Extensions

The extension spectral sequence introduced in Section 2 can be generalized for H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra. Consider a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y between two connective finite H​𝔽2\mathrm{H}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-synthetic spectra11 1 In our solution to the Kervaire invariant problem, we only consider finite synthetic spectra. However, the arguments in this section apply to any synthetic spectra for which the synthetic Adams spectral sequence strongly converges.. By filtering

0→π∗,∗​X→π∗,∗​fπ∗,∗​Y→00\to\pi_{*,*}X\xrightarrow{\pi_{*,*}f}\pi_{*,*}Y\to 0

using the Adams filtration, we obtain an ff-extension spectral sequence:

Es,t,w0f≅E∞s,t,w​(X)⊕E∞s,t,w​(Y)⟹ker⁡(π∗,∗​f)⊕coker⁡(π∗,∗​f)\prescript{f\!}{}{E}_{0}^{s,t,w}\cong E_{\infty}^{s,t,w}(X)\oplus E_{\infty}^{s,t,w}(Y)\Longrightarrow\Ker(\pi_{*,*}f)\oplus\Coker(\pi_{*,*}f)

with differential

dnf:Zs,t,wn−1f​(X)→E∞s+n,t+n,w​(Y)/Bs+n,t+n,wn−1f​(Y)d_{n}^{f}:\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}_{n-1}^{s,t,w}(X)\to E_{\infty}^{s+n,t+n,w}(Y)/\prescript{f\!}{}{B}_{n-1}^{s+n,t+n,w}(Y)

where Z∗,∗,∗∗f\prescript{f\!}{}{Z}_{*}^{*,*,*} and B∗,∗,∗∗f\prescript{f\!}{}{B}_{*}^{*,*,*} are analogous to the notations in Notation 2.2, with the addition of an extra degree.

In fact all the definitions and results in Section 2 remain valid in this synthetic setting, provided we include the extra weight degree in addition to the topological degree and ensure that all maps also preserve the weight degree. For convenience, we will not restate these results here but will occasionally refer to them and apply their synthetic versions when needed.

6. The Generalized Leibniz Rule and Generalized Mahowald Trick

Now, we introduce the theorem of the Generalized Leibniz Rule, a valuable tool for computing new Adams differentials.

Theorem 6.1 (Generalized Leibniz Rule).

Let f:X→Yf:X\to Y be a map between two classical spectra. Suppose that 2≤n≤r2\leq n\leq r, e⁡(f)≤m≤n−2+e⁡(f)e(f)\leq m\leq n-2+e(f), l≥e⁡(f)l\geq e(f), and we have

x∈Zr−1s,t​(X),y∈Zr−1−m+e⁡(f)s+m,t+m​(Y)x\in Z_{r-1}^{s,t}(X),\hskip 14.22636pty\in Z_{r-1-m+e(f)}^{s+m,t+m}(Y)
x∞∈Z∞s+r,t+r−1​(X),y∞∈Z∞s+r+l,t+r+l−1​(Y)x_{\infty}\in Z_{\infty}^{s+r,t+r-1}(X),\hskip 14.22636pty_{\infty}\in Z_{\infty}^{s+r+l,t+r+l-1}(Y)

and the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    dr​(x)=x∞d_{r}(x)=x_{\infty},

  2. (2)

    dmf,En​(x)=yd_{m}^{f,E_{n}}(x)=y,

  3. (3)

    dlf,E∞​(x∞)=y∞d_{l}^{f,E_{\infty}}(x_{\infty})=y_{\infty},

  4. (4)

    the differential in (1) has no crossing on the EnE_{n}-page or (2) has no crossing.

  5. (5)

    the differential in (3) has no crossing.

Then we have an Adams differential

dr+l−m​(y)=y∞.d_{r+l-m}(y)=y_{\infty}.
Proof.

Consider the commutative diagram of synthetic spectra

By condition (1) and Proposition 4.6, we have

(6.2) drδX​(x)=λr−n​x∞.d^{\delta_{X}}_{r}(x)=\lambda^{r-n}x_{\infty}.

By conditions (2) and (3), and Definition 5.4, we have

(6.3) dmf^n−1​(x)=λm−e⁡(f)​yd^{\hat{f}_{n-1}}_{m}(x)=\lambda^{m-e(f)}y

and

dlf^​(x∞)=λl−e⁡(f)​y∞,d^{\hat{f}}_{l}(x_{\infty})=\lambda^{l-e(f)}y_{\infty},

which implies

(6.4) dlf^​(λr−n​x∞)=λr+l−n−e⁡(f)​y∞.d^{\hat{f}}_{l}(\lambda^{r-n}x_{\infty})=\lambda^{r+l-n-e(f)}y_{\infty}.

Applying Proposition 4.16 and Proposition 5.10 to conditions (4) and (5), we know that the differential in (6.2) or (6.3) has no crossing, and that the differential in (6.4) has no crossing.

Therefore, we can apply Corollary 2.15 and obtain

dr+l−mδY​(λm−e⁡(f)​y)=λr+l−n−e⁡(f)​y∞.d^{\delta_{Y}}_{r+l-m}(\lambda^{m-e(f)}y)=\lambda^{r+l-n-e(f)}y_{\infty}.

By Remark 4.12, this is equivalent to

dr+l−m​(y)=y∞.d_{r+l-m}(y)=y_{\infty}.

∎

Remark 6.5.

We can further generalize Theorem 6.1 by using the conditions in Theorem 2.12 rather than those Corollary 2.15. We leave this generalization to the reader.

We emphasize that the no-crossing conditions in Theorem 6.1, the Generalized Leibniz Rule, are crucial. We first demonstrate the strength of the Generalized Leibniz Rule with Example 6.7, which uses a d2d_{2}-differential to prove a d3d_{3}-differential in the classical Adams spectral sequence. Additionally, Example 6.8 shows that, without the no-crossing condition, the conclusion could be false.

Remark 6.6.

A version of the Generalized Leibniz Rule without the no-crossing conditions is presented in the synthetic setting in Chua’s work [19, Theorem 12.9]. However, there is no doubt that this version is incorrect. Indeed, Example 6.8 is a counter-example to Chua’s theorem. For further details, see Remark 6.10.

Remark 6.9.

As noted in Example 5.8(4) and Example 5.13(4), the essential (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extension:

d1f,E∞​(d0)=h0​d0,d_{1}^{f,E_{\infty}}(d_{0})=h_{0}d_{0},

is a crossing for both the (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extension,

d2f,E∞​(h0​h32)=0,d_{2}^{f,E_{\infty}}(h_{0}h_{3}^{2})=0,

and the inessential (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extension:

d2f,E∞​(h0​h32)=h0​d0.d_{2}^{f,E_{\infty}}(h_{0}h_{3}^{2})=h_{0}d_{0}.

This indicates that, in Example 6.8, if we were to disregard the no-crossing condition (5), and apply the Generalized Leibniz Rule to these two cases of the (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extensions, we would arrive at two conflicting classical statements:

d3​(h0​h4)=0,d3​(h0​h4)=h0​d0.d_{3}(h_{0}h_{4})=0,\ d_{3}(h_{0}h_{4})=h_{0}d_{0}.
Remark 6.10.

In Chua’s work [19, Theorem 12.9], it is stated that for a synthetic map α:X→Y\alpha:X\rightarrow Y, and an element x∈π∗,∗​X/λx\in\pi_{*,*}X/\lambda, there exists a differential from a maximal α\alpha-extension of xx to a maximal α\alpha-extension of dr​(x)d_{r}(x). According to [19, Definition 12.5], a maximal α\alpha-extension of x′x^{\prime} is defined as α⁡[x′]\alpha[x^{\prime}], where [x′][x^{\prime}] represents a lift of x′x^{\prime} to the Er′E_{r^{\prime}}-page, chosen such that α⁡[x′]\alpha[x^{\prime}] is the most λ\lambda-divisible among all such lifts.

In the context of Example 6.8, let r=2,r′=∞r=2,r^{\prime}=\infty,

α=[h0]:S0,1→S0,0,\alpha=[h_{0}]:S^{0,1}\rightarrow S^{0,0},

and consider x=h4x=h_{4} in Ext, with x′=d2​(x)=h0​h32x^{\prime}=d_{2}(x)=h_{0}h_{3}^{2}.

As noted in Example 5.8(4), the (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extension:

d2f,E∞​(h0​h32)=0d_{2}^{f,E_{\infty}}(h_{0}h_{3}^{2})=0

is equivalent to the existence of a synthetic homotopy class [h0​h32][h_{0}h_{3}^{2}] in π14,17​S0,0\pi_{14,17}S^{0,0}, such that

[h0​h32]⋅[h0]=0​in​π14,18​S0,0.[h_{0}h_{3}^{2}]\cdot[h_{0}]=0\ \text{in}\ \pi_{14,18}S^{0,0}.

Similarly, the inessential (f,E∞)(f,E_{\infty})-extension:

d2f,E∞​(h0​h32)=h0​d0d_{2}^{f,E_{\infty}}(h_{0}h_{3}^{2})=h_{0}d_{0}

implies the existence of another synthetic homotopy class [h0​h32][h_{0}h_{3}^{2}] in π14,17​S0,0\pi_{14,17}S^{0,0}, such that

[h0​h32]⋅[h0]=[h0​d0]​in​π14,18​S0,0.[h_{0}h_{3}^{2}]\cdot[h_{0}]=[h_{0}d_{0}]\ \text{in}\ \pi_{14,18}S^{0,0}.

Between these two lifts of h0​h32h_{0}h_{3}^{2}, the first [h0​h32][h_{0}h_{3}^{2}] is clearly the maximal [h0][h_{0}]-extension according to Chua’s definition [19, Definition 12.5]. Consequently, the incorrect version of the Generalized Leibniz Rule in [19, Theorem 12.9], would lead to an incorrect conclusion:

Next, we discuss the Generalized Mahowald Trick.

In order to apply the Generalized Leibniz Rule, we need to provide a method for computing extensions on specific Adams EkE_{k}-pages, such as the (f,E3)(f,E_{3})-extension d2f,E3​(h0​h42)=h0​pd_{2}^{f,E_{3}}(h_{0}h_{4}^{2})=h_{0}p in Example 6.7. This is provided by Theorem 6.12 (the Generalized Mahowald Trick). The crux of the proof of the Generalized Mahowald Trick lies in the following lemma.

Lemma 6.11 (May [46]).

Let X→Y→Z→Σ​XX\to Y\to Z\to\Sigma X and X′→Y′→Z′→Σ​X′X^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime}\to Z^{\prime}\to\Sigma X^{\prime} be distinguished triangles of (synthetic) spectra. By smashing these distinguished triangles together, we obtain the following commutative diagram of cofiber sequences:

If a∈πn​(X∧Z′)a\in\pi_{n}(X\wedge Z^{\prime}) and b∈πn​(Y∧Y′)b\in\pi_{n}(Y\wedge Y^{\prime}) map to the same element in πn​(Y∧Z′)\pi_{n}(Y\wedge Z^{\prime}), then there exists c∈πn​(Z∧X′)c\in\pi_{n}(Z\wedge X^{\prime}) such that

  1. (1)

  2. (2)

    aa and cc map to the same element via boundary maps in πn−1​(X∧X′)\pi_{n-1}(X\wedge X^{\prime}).

The proof follows directly from [46, Lemma 4.6].

In fact, consider VV in Axiom TC3 of [46, Section 4] and the corresponding commutative diagram. By [46, Lemma 4.6] we know that VV is the pull back of the following diagram.

Since aa and bb map to the same element in πn​(Y∧Z′)\pi_{n}(Y\wedge Z^{\prime}), we know that we can find v∈Vv\in V such that vv maps to aa in πn​(X∧Z′)\pi_{n}(X\wedge Z^{\prime}) and bb in πn​(Y∧Y′)\pi_{n}(Y\wedge Y^{\prime}). Then we let c=j3​(v)∈πn​(Z∧X′)c=j_{3}(v)\in\pi_{n}(Z\wedge X^{\prime}), where j3:V→Z∧X′j_{3}:V\rightarrow Z\wedge X^{\prime} is the map in the commutative diagram in Axiom TC3 of [46, Section 4]. This lemma follows from the commutativity of the diagram. ∎

We refer to Theorem 6.12 as the Generalized Mahowald Trick, as this approach was first utilized by Mahowald and his collaborators in various works (see, for example, [44]), particularly in the case where m1=l1=0m_{1}=l_{1}=0. The synthetic setting advances this method by allowing for the consideration of cases where m1>0,l1>0m_{1}>0,l_{1}>0 as well.

Remark 6.17.

Several versions of classical generalizations of Mahowald’s original trick appear in the literature and are often referred to as geometric boundary theorems. Notable examples include the works of Behrens [8], and Ma [41].

Remark 6.18.

A synthetic generalization of the Mahowald Trick, again lacking any no-crossing conditions, is also presented in Chua’s work [19, Theorem 12.11]. This version is also incorrect for similar reasons.

Theorem 7.3 is proved using the quadratic construction on a map from the mod 2 Moore spectrum to the sphere spectrum, where the restriction on the bottom cell is θ5\theta_{5}. Therefore, it is necessary to use a θ5\theta_{5} of order 2.

Notably, [56, 29] confirms that all classical θ5\theta_{5}’s indeed have order 2. To prove Proposition 7.8, we first establish Lemmas 7.10 and 7.11, which demonstrate that the existential statements (4)(4) and (5)(5) in Proposition 7.8 are equivalent to their corresponding universal statements (4′)(4^{\prime}) and (5′)(5^{\prime}).

Lemma 7.10.

Lemma 7.11.

By the rigidity Theorem 3.6 of the synthetic Adams spectral sequence for S0,0/(λ⁡[h2])S^{0,0}/(\lambda[h_{2}]), we know that the element λ4​h1​h4​x109,12​[0]\lambda^{4}h_{1}h_{4}x_{109,12}[0] must be killed by a synthetic Adams differential, which corresponds to to a statement that in the classical Adams spectral sequence of S0/νS^{0}/\nu, the element h1​h4​x109,12​[0]h_{1}h_{4}x_{109,12}[0] must be killed by a drd_{r}-differential for r≤5r\leq 5.

However, from Table 1 (obtained from [38] [37], and can be visualized from [35]), in the classical Adams spectral sequence of S0/νS^{0}/\nu, the element h1​h4​x109,12​[0]h_{1}h_{4}x_{109,12}[0] is not killed by any drd_{r} for r≤5r\leq 5 (from the range of 9≤s≤149\leq s\leq 14 in stem 126). Therefore, we arrive at a contradiction. ∎

8. Appendix: The classical Adams spectral sequence in the range 122≤t−s≤127,s≤25122\leq t-s\leq 127,s\leq 25

We provide a brief overview of Lin’s computer program for computing Adams differentials and extensions. The program’s functionality for propagating differentials and extensions relies on the following data:

  • •

    The Adams E2E_{2}-pages of a collection of CW spectra.

  • •

    Maps between these E2E_{2}-pages.

  • •

    Adams d2d_{2}-differentials for certain CW spectra.

  • •

    There are three manually added differentials: d5​h024​h6=h02​P6​d0d_{5}h_{0}^{24}h_{6}=h_{0}^{2}P^{6}d_{0} and
    d6​h055​h7=h02​x126,60d_{6}h_{0}^{55}h_{7}=h_{0}^{2}x_{126,60} in the Adams spectral sequence of S0S^{0} (from the image of JJ), and d3​v216=β5​gd_{3}v_{2}^{16}=\beta^{5}g in the Adams spectral sequence of 𝑡𝑚𝑓\mathit{tmf}, derived from power operations (Bruner–Rognes [12]).

Detailed descriptions of these data are available in [37]. Lin’s program extends these results by computing additional Adams differentials using tools such as the Leibniz rule, naturality, the Generalized Leibniz Rule, and the Generalized Mahowald Trick. All computed differentials and extensions are accessible via interactive plots [35].

Moreover, the proofs provided in [37] offer more information than the interactive plots. These proofs include numerous disproofs of potential differentials, even for cases where the differentials remain unresolved. For example, consider

x126,21∈E221,126+21​(S0).x_{126,21}\in E_{2}^{21,126+21}(S^{0}).

The spectral sequence plot for S0S^{0} shows that x126,21x_{126,21} survives to the E4E_{4}-page, but the value of d4​(x126,21)d_{4}(x_{126,21}) undetermined. By analyzing the proofs in [37], we observe that many potential values for d4​(x126,21)d_{4}(x_{126,21}) have been ruled out. Consequently, we conclude:

d4​(x126,21)=x125,25,2+x125,25+g4​Δ​h1​g+possibly ​d02​e0​g​B4.d_{4}(x_{126,21})=x_{125,25,2}+x_{125,25}+g^{4}\Delta h_{1}g+\text{possibly }d_{0}^{2}e_{0}gB_{4}.
